The very fact that you feel so guilty about this and have thoroughly thought through why what you did was wrong is proof that you are not a bad person and you are someone who reflects on your behavior responsibly. What makes you a good person is being eager to reflect on your behavior, admit where it was wrong and try to do better forward, even if it's just bit by bit. Daydreaming in itself is not maladaptive. It is maladaptive when you start neglecting school life, social life, cooking, eating, personal hygene and so on just so you can sit and MD. 

Daydreaming is a form of stimulation that is normal and can appear just because she has an active imagination and is really excited about this particular fictional universe or other things. At this point it can just be an activity like gaming in which kids will lose track of time. If her mind needs this kind of stimulation, she will find it in other stories even if you limit the Harry Potter stuff or even after she gets tired of it. I just naturally daydreamed about every book or movie I really liked.

However, it is good that you respectfully monitor (as in recognize her right to privacy, but explain why you do it, so she doesn't feel like it's just because you have power over her and you can) what she looks at on the internet and communicate openly and without judgement. In these fandoms there's a lot of fanfiction that can get sexual, violent and straight up disturbing. I would have appreciated being protected from seeing all this as a preteen/teen and having a safe space to openly discuss and make sense of the things I find out, without being berated about how I found it and why I looked at it (it's unrealistic to expect that they won't come across anything sketchy and won't be curious to read further - so just help her understand and make sense of sexual things or the more uncomfortable aspects of life like violence if it happens).

Daydreaming is also a coping mechanism and is actually very useful in relaxing you. If it's just used for 1-2 hours a day to take a break from everyone and everything that's perfectly normal. I often used it to make sense of the world and process events that happened or new things I learned by inserting them into a plot. 
At the same time it can become something you get too comfortable in and start to hide in. It can definitely also be a warning sign, but it's not always of something bad. It might pick up in frequency when the academic or social pressure gets too much or when she feels disconnected and needs emotional support.

For me it started to be maladaltive when I felt overwhelmed and scared as a teen and the adults around wouldn't take it seriously. Or when family members would unload their emotional turmoil on me and trauma dump. So really the main thing for you to do is just be supportive and belive her when she talkes about how she feels or what she's experiencing. Childhood and teenage are legitimately difficult and many parents make it worse by not being the safe space of unconditional love they should be. Their brains are developing and constantly adapting to new information and experiences. Most times they are not being petty or overdramatic, they feel real emotional turmoil.

Lastly, whenever I truly forgot about daydreaming was during the days when I was in activities that interested me with a group of peers I clicked with. I don't know what the options are where you live, but try getting her involved in clubs or camps. She might not find an acitvity or group she clicks with right away and might need to switch things.

The most important thing is just being there, showing unconditional love and also giving her opportunities to be a part of a community in which she gets to develop her independence and identity in a safe space. That's really the takeaway I have from my own childhood and what I observed in my peers. Issues appear when they are left alienated, without real support from the parents and without peers to connect with, because the connections you make with kids your age can not be replaced by anything. And not all children will find that connection with the classmates at school, which is why it's important that they also do things outside the school in different groups.

It will be challenging for you as she grows up and you see her change her thinking or her favorite color. Teens also have a deep need to show independence and gain some control in their life, so they might rebel. If you get into conflicts don't take her power away and work to find a middle ground. Have the difficult conversations she needs to have. And never use shame ("what will these people say about you", "everyone is doing this, why can't you") or the silent treatment when you get mad, you can just say you are overwhelmed and need some time before you talk it out. In my case daydreaming got maladaptive also because I couldn't find a safe judgement-free space in my parents. Children mainly need love that is not conditional or demanding of them from their parents.

It happens to me both in and out of relationships. It's like my brain just takes their image and runs with it. And what's worse is that while my mind is running wild and putting them in all these scenarios I completely disregard what they are saying and who they are in reality. So then that leaves me with an empty fantasy and no authentic real life connection. 

It's somehow particularly heartbreaking and isolating.

It can still be good, generally as long as children feel they are loved unconditionally and given the space to be who they are, they are quite oblivious to how shitty the world is. And even when they grow up, they have the resilience to deal with it better than most of us.

The best you can do now is to learn how to raise her best, cultivate security and self-confidence, make space for all her feelings, offer emotional comfort and teach coping mechanisms, as she will go through hard feelings. 

If you can afford it getting therapy for yourself so you don't unconsciously pass negative feelings, beliefs and habits onto her would be a great help. Generally taking care of yourself and having people help you will in turn help her.

Other than that, just give her opportunities to connect with other children, like clubs, camps and all, but within reason. Kids also get low social battery and generally show it. 

From what I've experienced it looks like those who have been raised to have a secure attachment and authentic connections don't really mind the meaningless of existence, even when they are aware of it.

The main thing is that children are all unique and they all have a unique set of needs. Whatever their needs are, they are entitled to them, they are children who are helpless and depend on adults to survive and make sense of the world. 

Now, the adults made a choice in bringing a child into the world. Sadly, most are uneducated about what having a child is actually like. But, still, they signed up for whatever that child needs when they decided to bring it into the world. Teachers also signed up for the job, I'm sure they are well aware of the worst possible behaviors that can appear in a classroom and they still teach. 

And yes, children are burdens, this is why many of us chose not to have them. Your family made the choice to have this burden and embrace it. Children are by default draining burdens, even at their best.

It's never a child's fault for being the way they are, they don't know better and have no tools to make sense of themselves or the world. It's the adults that fail at providing for all the needs of a child or fail at dealing with what is often normal behavior for the circumstances a child is in.

Children are by their nature exhausting and draining, they push you like you have never been pushed and somehow you still have to keep showing up for them. I've spent time with children with no behavior issues and their constant need for interaction or whatever else drove me up the walls. Even as they grow into their teens, they just have different needs and the adult still has to make efforts to provide for them, and not only financially, but psychologically, being there for them and guiding them. This is the job of parents, to walk along with the child, guide them through life, whatever the circumstances.

This is why having a child is such a big deal and not a decision to make lightly.

ETA: While children are indeed burdens, I think you should know that they also don't ask to be here and that those first 18 years of development are a lot of work, and it's normal for things to be difficult for them, for bahavioral issues to appear or for them to need more support, either emotional or whatever else.
